synopsis: The booklet presents genetic algorithms, NSGA-II, Bayesian optimization and gradient-free search as ways to tune settings through slow simulations; it matches evolutionary methods to braking trade-offs, Bayesian optimization to expensive HIL or physical evaluations, and response surfaces to a few smooth parameters [f14417, f14427, f14428, f14425]. Evolutionary methods, including NSGA-II attributed to Deb and colleagues in 2002, expose the Pareto frontier and parallelise readily, but require many evaluations and leave the acceptable trade-off to policy [f14420, f6970, f7319]. Bayesian optimization uses surrogate predictions and uncertainty for sample-efficient trial selection, but weakens beyond roughly 20 parameters or around discontinuities and can wrongly extrapolate safety [f6974, f7325, f6979]. Although gradient-free search suits threshold-like braking outcomes, this does not remove Bayesian methods’ discontinuity limitations; evolutionary tuning also needs nested validation and independent confirmation to control over-fitting [f14418, f7325, f7320, f7321]. Transfer methods reuse a tuned machine model and search residual settings, but risk negative transfer, while safe multi-task optimization remains research rather than established heavy-machinery practice [f7031, f7341, f7034]. The evidence is predominantly generic engineering: the booklet identifies no specific off-road evidence for evolutionary or Bayesian tuning and no off-road collision-avoidance application of the discussed transfer methods [f7322, f7328, f7035].
